author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: Permission for Privacy
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
The chalkboard in Lanternwell Square had acquired a new column.

It stood beside the bakery menu under the heading *Who's with Jasper?* Someone had drawn six little hearts and written the names of people I cared about, with blank spaces for dates and guesses.

I stared until the letters stopped making sense.

Mara came out carrying a tray of rolls. She saw the board and went still.

"That's not mine."

"I know."

"I was going to wipe it off, but I thought you should decide whether you wanted to see it first."

I swallowed. I was furious with the person who'd written it, but I was also strangely ashamed. The chalkboard made my life look like a game people could follow, score, and argue about over breakfast.

"Would you give me the cloth?" I asked.

Mara handed it over.

I wiped the names away.

Behind me someone said, "Oh. I thought it was just a joke."

I turned. A man I recognized from the market stood holding a basket of apples. He looked embarrassed rather than cruel.

"Whose joke?" I asked.

"People were talking. You and Maui, and the others. We wondered how it all worked."

"Then you could have asked me a question that didn't require exposing six people's private lives."

He shifted the basket. "I didn't think anyone would mind."

"You didn't ask them."

I heard my voice grow sharper. I wanted to make him feel exactly as small as the board had made me feel. I was not proud of that.

Maui arrived before I could say anything else. He looked at the damp board, then at my face.

His eyes followed the six hearts down the board. I watched the easy grin drain out of his face.

"Well," he said, very softly. "Whoever drew this has a powerful imagination and absolutely terrible manners."

Mini Maui came running across his upper arm carrying an imaginary giant eraser. The real Maui looked ready to do the same thing with his hook and perhaps the entire board.

I wanted that anger on my side. I didn't want him to turn it into a public spectacle that would make the story even harder to escape.

"Jasper," he said, voice suddenly big enough to make passersby turn, "I could give a speech so magnificent they would never gossip again."

"Please don't."

He closed his mouth, clearly in pain.

"Fine. No speech. Extremely difficult, but fine."

I saw the impulse hadn't gone anywhere. His fists were tight, and he was watching the man who'd drawn the board. But when I began to speak, he backed up and let people hear me. He wasn't calm. He was choosing not to make his anger more important than mine.

"What happened?"

I told him.

His jaw tightened. For a moment I saw the old Maui, ready to turn the whole square into a battlefield because someone had embarrassed a person he loved.

He looked at me. "What do you want?"

"Not a speech from you," I said quickly. "Please."

He breathed in, then out. "All right."

I asked Neri for five minutes at the community notice board. A few people gathered, including several who had seen the chalkboard before it was erased. I kept the account plain.

"I'm ethically non-monogamous," I said. "I prefer polyamory. The people in my relationships know that. They each make their own choices, and some of those choices are private."

A woman raised her hand. "So you don't have to tell everyone?"

"No. Neither do you."

"What about fairness?"

"Fairness means honesty with the people affected, respecting consent, and keeping the commitments we actually make. It doesn't mean putting everyone's schedule on a public board."

Someone asked whether my partners liked each other.

"That's their business," I said. "Some have worked together. Some want space. None of them owes the square a performance."

The man with the apples had stayed near the edge of the crowd. He looked down at his basket.

I could have called him out by name.

I didn't.

Instead I asked the council to put a privacy rule beside the public festival guidelines: notice boards were for community business, not speculation about residents' romantic lives. Mara added a second rule about not writing personal contact information without permission.

Neri approved the notice.

It wasn't a law against gossip. People would still talk. But it established a boundary the community could enforce in the spaces it maintained.

Later, I found Maui at Tideglass repairing a lantern hook.

"Are you angry?" I asked.

"Yes."

"At me?"

"At the board."

I leaned against the post. "You didn't say much."

"You asked me not to."

"Was that difficult?"

"Extremely. I had three speeches ready."

I laughed despite myself.

He put down the hook.

"About the speech you heroically saved me from giving," Maui said. "Does this mean if somebody asks what we do at home, I can tell them to mind their own coconuts?"

"Yes."

"Sometimes I don't want to hear every detail about the others. Sometimes I do need to know when our plans change. And sometimes—" He scowled at the hook. "Sometimes my brain insists I should *win* at being loved. Which is ridiculous. And terrible for my winning record."

I took his hand.

"You can ask. I can decide what belongs to me to share. If it belongs to someone else too, I ask them first."

He frowned.

"What about kisses?"

"Those are ours when they're between us. We can talk about them if we both want. They're not the village's property."

He smiled slowly.

Mara came back across the square with a fresh price board, still looking upset about what someone had written on the chalk.

"I was thinking," she said. "Maybe the notice boards should be separated. People keep putting personal messages beside the public safety information because it's the only place everybody knows to look."

Neri, who had been updating the departure instructions, stopped to listen.

"A public board for services," they said. "A private message shelf for things addressed to one person. The shelf would need a way to refuse unwanted notes, too."

"And no list of who collects what," I added.

Mara nodded. "I don't want the bakery becoming a gossip desk."

We worked out a small plan that afternoon. The service board would hold prices, closures, community meeting times and voluntarily credited work. Personal messages could be left in sealed envelopes through the registrar, who could return anything unwanted without posting it in public.

Pip offered to paint a sign. Edda made them check that the new shelf could be reached without blocking the walkway. A new rule wasn't finished just because someone had written it in attractive letters.

Maui held the ladder while the sign went up.

"I could give a speech about everyone's freedom," he whispered.

"I know."

"Would it be bad?"

"Probably magnificent."

He grinned.

"And unnecessary."

He sighed theatrically, but let Pip fasten the last corner. When the square was tidy again, he reached for my hand and waited.

"I like that you can tell me what you want private," he said.

"Even when you want to know?"

"Especially then. I may still be curious."

"I'll still tell you the things that affect us. You don't need a public scoreboard to know I care."

We stood beneath the new sign while people walked past without noticing us. It was wonderfully ordinary. The next time somebody wanted to announce who Jasper had kissed, the town at least had a clear reason to say that wasn't what the public board was for.

"Good."

The sunset lit the signal post in amber. I could hear Lio arguing with Fen about a skiff measurement and the bakery bell sounding faintly from the square. There was a whole life around us, full of people who deserved to have some parts remain their own.

Maui stepped closer.

"May I kiss you somewhere nobody's taking notes?"

"Yes."

We went home by the upper path, laughing when the wind tried to steal his cloak. At the door he kissed me, then again after I pulled him closer. The rest of the evening was private, the door closed because we had chosen it.

Before we left, Neri caught us beside the fountain.

"I have a problem," they said, carrying a second sheet of paper. "We keep an arrival book so people can be found when crossings go wrong. If we stop taking names, we lose the safety record. But if we publish who went where—"

"We do the chalkboard all over again," I finished.

Edda, passing toward the archive, stopped to listen. She pointed out that the registrar's desk couldn't be reached without stairs after the side path flooded. That made an emergency contact fairly useless if the person who needed the record couldn't get inside.

We wrote a new rule together. The public board would show Threadway closures and available services, not visitors' destinations. A traveler could give Neri a restricted emergency contact, refuse to list an unrelated private appointment, and request correction without broadcasting their business. If someone challenged an entry, a second registrar would review it.

Maui studied the page. "That sounds like a lot of work just to stop people being nosy."

"It's work we should have done before the board hurt somebody," I said.

He didn't argue. Instead he held the ladder while Neri pinned the notice in a place Edda could actually read.

The man with the apples approached again.

"I'm sorry," he said. "I made it a joke because I didn't think about the people underneath it."

I was still angry. "Don't do it again."

"I won't."

I wasn't required to make him feel better. He went back to his market stall, and I went home with Maui.

On the path, Maui touched my wrist. "Ask about the ledger tomorrow?"

"Yes."

"Ask about your other partners?"

"Only what affects our agreements, like we said."

He grinned. "I am becoming a very sophisticated man."

"You held a ladder."

"Heroically."

I kissed his cheek, which managed to shut him up for nearly ten seconds.


The next morning the chalkboard held the day's bread prices and the tide warning, nothing else.

There were six hearts still faintly visible beneath the damp surface.

I didn't erase them again.

The boundary was the important part. The trace of somebody's mistake could stay without deciding what happened next.
